GNG Electronics( Cmp 704) is a company that buys used laptops, desktops, and other information technology devices, repairs them, and sells them as refurbished products under the brand Electronics Bazaar. It is the largest organised refurbisher of laptops and desktops in India and also sells in many other countries. The company offers warranties of up to three years in India and one year in international markets. Its refurbished devices are sold at roughly one-third the price of new devices.The company is linked to the growth of artificial intelligence because large investments in AI data centres are changing the supply of computer memory. Memory makers are shifting a large part of their production capacity to high-bandwidth memory, which is used in AI servers. This has reduced the supply of ordinary DRAM and storage used in standard personal computers. As a result, prices of RAM and related components have risen sharply. Reports note that prices of certain DDR5 memory modules rose several times between late 2025 and early 2026, and the cost of new computers has increased by around 20 percent or more in many markets. Industry estimates suggest that new PC shipments could fall in 2026 because of these shortages, and higher prices are expected to continue for some time.Higher prices of new devices benefit GNG Electronics in two ways. First, more buyers, including companies and institutions, turn to refurbished products because they remain much cheaper while still meeting basic performance needs. Second, the company can raise the prices of its own refurbished devices to some extent as new-device prices rise, which supports better realisations and margins. The company also buys used equipment in advance when it expects component prices to increase, which helps protect its supply and can improve profitability. Laptops form the largest part of its sales.

Financials 
In the financial year ended March 2026, consolidated revenue rose 34 percent year on year to ₹1,891 crore, EBITDA margin improved to 10.6 percent, and profit after tax nearly doubled to ₹132 crore, with the profit margin rising to 7 percent from 4.9 percent in the previous year. Management initially guided for about 25 percent revenue growth in the following year and at least a 50 basis point expansion in the profit-after-tax margin; after the first quarter of the next year, which showed revenue growth of about 32 percent, it raised the full-year revenue growth guidance to 30 percent and the expected profit-margin expansion to 75–100 basis points.

text:
Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

Who won this round, Musk or Altman?

IRAN:

Trump said in Texas on Thursday night that the war with the Islamic Republic would end “very soon” and that Tehran must “make the right and smart decision” or it would lose its current position, adding that Washington was still pursuing negotiations. (Iran International)

The US sent two additional Patriot batteries last month to protect a Saudi oil facility and a Qatari gas facility, according to two US officials and a regional source. The deployments were intended to reassure both countries ahead of possible renewed strikes on Iran. (Axios)  

Iran has averaged roughly 30 drone and 10 anti-ship missile attacks weekly since August, according to a Western security official cited by NYT; at least four commercial vessels were hit in the past 10 days. Many attacks have been unsuccessful. (NYT)  

Iran’s proposed Hormuz bill would bar Israeli and hostile-state vessels, plus military cargoes; other ships would need Armed Forces General Staff permission, parliament’s national-security spokesman told Tasnim. It still requires a parliamentary vote and further legal approval. (Tasnim)  

OSINT accounts reported explosions/fire at Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu North crude export terminal which could not be verified. (OSINT report)  

The Saudi-led coalition said a Houthi drone struck Madinah’s Taibah power distribution station on Tuesday, which supplies the Prophet’s Mosque. A transformer was taken offline, although the coalition said the electricity network was unaffected. (BBG) 

Bloomberg interviews tanker captains who described transiting Hormuz under US military protection with lights and communications switched off, hugging Oman’s coast. Shipping executives estimate roughly a one-in-20 chance of a vessel being hit during a crossing, Bloomberg reports. (BBG)   

Recovering Hormuz traffic isn’t translating into cheaper fuel: Middle East refined-product exports remain around 40% below prewar levels, according to JPMorgan. WSJ reports freight costs, refinery disruption and depleted inventories are keeping inflation pressure elevated. (WSJ) 

Banks raised their average Q4 Brent forecast to $90.22/bbl from $78.92, and WTI to $85.47 from $74.62, in a WSJ survey. Macquarie said it struggles to see a timely, comprehensive and lasting resolution to the Iran conflict. (WSJ)   

Jera CEO Yukio Kani told Bloomberg TV he does not expect Qatari LNG supplies to return soon. He warned that low European storage and the January ban on Russian LNG imports could push spot prices higher into winter. (BBG) 

Fuel subsidies could exceed $1tn this year as governments shield consumers from the Iran war’s energy shock, a UNDP report warned. Higher borrowing costs and El Niño are making relief harder to sustain, with the combined pressures projected to peak in early 2027. (BBG)   

MACRO:

Unwinding leveraged hedge-fund trades intensified selling in French debt and spilled into Italian and Greek bonds, traders told WSJ. The French–German yield spread reached 140bp, its widest since the eurozone debt crisis, while Treasurys benefited from demand for safety. (WSJ)  

Fed’s Logan (voter) said rates need to rise another “50 basis points or more,” in prepared remarks at the Dallas Fed. However, she said rising Treasury term premiums could slow the economy and reduce the amount of monetary tightening required. (BBG)  

Bloomberg’s payrolls survey points to September jobs growth of 90k versus 162k previously. T. Rowe Price’s Steve Boothe said a near-zero or negative print, alongside weaker wages, would likely be needed to drive a Treasury rally given entrenched expectations for further Fed hikes. (BBG)  

Heavy Treasury shorts are creating pressure in repo, with the current 10-year note’s repo rate trading as low as 2.70%, according to Curvature Securities. Its Scott Skyrm expects volatility to persist over the next two weeks as the upcoming auction attracts further shorts. (BBG)

Global corporate-bond spreads widened around 5bps this week, the most since March, to their widest in six months as record issuance tests demand. Asian investment-grade spreads widened another 2–4bps early Friday, traders said. (BBG)

The equal-weight S&P 500 is heading for a seventh consecutive weekly decline, something previously seen only in 2002 and 2022, according to Bloomberg data. AI megacaps are masking growing damage from higher yields across small caps, banks and utilities. (BBG)  

Citadel Securities’ Scott Rubner turns more constructive on US equities into Q4, citing reduced leverage, lighter systematic positioning and returning buybacks. He sees early-quarter weakness as an opportunity to rebuild exposure. (Citadel Securities)  

Ramp economist Ara Kharazian says AI spending is falling despite rising usage in its latest data, driven “almost exclusively by competition between OpenAI + Anthropic” and cheaper models. He clarified that the chart covers API spending, including Bedrock/GCP usage, and that spending peaked in July. (X)  

Jay Clayton is the likely AI-czar pick and could retain his intelligence role, CBS reports; the White House called the reporting “baseless speculation”. (CBS)  

Tokyo core CPI accelerated to 2.7% Y/Y in September versus 2.3% expected and 1.8% previously. Inflation excluding fresh food and energy rose to 3.0% from 2.0%, reinforcing the BoJ’s concerns about an inflation overshoot. (BBG)  

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell as much as 3%, its biggest decline since March, as trading resumed after the holiday. HSBC dropped 5.7%, with higher yields, potential UK bank taxes and disappointment over China’s stimulus weighing on sentiment. (BBG)  

South Korean CPI eased to 2.9% Y/Y in September, matching expectations, from 3.1%; core inflation slowed to 2.8% from 3.4%. The BoK said underlying pressures had picked up after adjusting for temporary effects and expects headline inflation around 3% in October. (BBG)  

Australia’s 10-year yield premium over Treasuries narrowed to about 12bps as markets bet the RBA is closer to finishing its hiking cycle than the Fed. Barrenjoey and Westpac expect convergence, while NAB sees scope for the spread to turn negative. (BBG)  

New Zealand’s governing National Party pledged to require large data centres to match their electricity demand with new generation and backup supply if re-elected. The requirements would be conditions of project approval, energy spokesperson Simeon Brown said. (BBG)  

France’s fiscal deterioration is driving investors out of its assets, Bloomberg reports, with the 10-year yield near 4.9% and its premium over Bunds at 141bps. Nomura sees that spread potentially reaching 200bps by end-2027 as political fragmentation obstructs deficit reduction. (BBG)

Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management sold all its French government bonds over fiscal concerns, shifting proceeds mainly into Bunds and partly into short-dated JGBs, portfolio manager Shinji Kunibe told Bloomberg. (BBG)

Brazil’s Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro remain statistically tied ahead of Sunday’s election, according to Datafolha. Lula leads 48%–45% in a runoff scenario and 42%–38% in the first round; a second round would take place on 25 October. (BBG)  

GEOPOLITICAL:

Russia is preparing a large-scale campaign of strikes on the Ukrainian energy system, according to a document cited by NYT. Among the potential targets are electrical substations, hydroelectric power plants, thermal power plants and boiler houses. Separately, the plan mentions strikes on Ukraine's three operating nuclear power plants. (NYT)

Putin instructed military leaders in September to abandon the rules of war, according to intercepted intelligence cited by Ukrainian President Zelenskyy in an FT interview. Zelenskyy said the order led to a sharp increase in Russian strikes on civilian targets, including schools, hospitals, data centres and bridges, aimed at instilling fear and pressuring the population amid static front lines. (FT)

Ukraine said it used its domestically produced FP-7, a hard to stop long range missile, in combat for the first time, targeting Russian forces in occupied Ukraine. Zelensky said the next priority is production; WSJ notes the strike’s success remains unclear and manufacturing capacity is constrained. (WSJ)  

Russia’s Samara oil distribution station reportedly caught fire following an overnight Ukrainian drone attack. The extent of damage and any throughput impact remained unverified. (Kyiv Independent)  

The Volgograd oil refinery was also identified as a likely target of overnight Ukrainian strikes, with fire reported; no confirmed production-loss figures. (Kyiv Independent) 

Romania reported that an object, possibly a drone, fell near Plauru and caused a fire during Russian attacks across the Ukrainian border. No casualties or material damage reported. (Romanian Defence Ministry)   

Hungary has no plans to supply troops or weapons to Ukraine, Deputy Foreign Minister Gyorgy Velkey told Bloomberg. Support will remain limited to energy and humanitarian assistance despite the new government’s closer alignment with the EU. (BBG)  

Taiwan received its first two F-16 Block 70 fighters from a 66-aircraft US order placed in 2019, after years of delays. Defence Minister Wellington Koo said further deliveries would follow before year-end. (BBG)  

EQUITIES:

Amazon is seeking to offload about $8B of advanced Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips to external investors through a special-purpose vehicle to strengthen its balance sheet, according to FT sources. Amazon would spin off chips deployed in US data centres into the SPV, lease them back, and offer up to a 10% equity stake in the entity while retaining no ownership. (FT)

Broadcom’s banking syndicate is beginning to assemble $60bn of AI-chip financing for Anthropic and other customers, according to Bloomberg sources. The package comprises $42bn of senior debt and $18bn of junior debt led by Blackstone, which plans to commit $9bn itself. (BBG)  

Intel’s 14A process is attracting evaluation interest from major customers including Apple, Amazon, Nvidia and AMD as they assess alternatives to TSMC, DigiTimes reports. No formal orders have been confirmed. (DigiTimes)  

Bloomberg’s chip-smuggling investigation reports growing official scrutiny of gaps in Nvidia’s customer checks as restricted processors reach China through Southeast Asia. Nvidia has not been accused of violating export controls and says prosecutors allege diversion of less than 0.5% of its products. (BBG)  

Chinese state-backed Semi-Tech Leasing financed purchases of servers containing restricted Nvidia B300 chips, regulatory documents reviewed by Bloomberg show. One contract covers 32 Asus servers; Nvidia said it is investigating with its equipment-manufacturing customer. (BBG) 

Nvidia is testing glass-cloth-free PCB materials with suppliers, including PTFE and hydrocarbon resins, to meet AI-server signal requirements. DigiTimes says the target application is the Rubin Ultra NVL576 switch, scheduled for mass production in H2 2027. (DigiTimes)  

Micron’s Taiwan chairman says memory supply should tighten further in 2027–28, with most 2027 HBM capacity already covered by long-term agreements at prices above 2026 levels. Some customer contracts extend into 2030–31. (Commercial Times)  

New Mexico is seeking $35–40bn in penalties from Meta after a jury found it misled consumers over Facebook data privacy in a Cambridge Analytica-related case. Meta wants penalties capped at $3.45bn; the judge expects to rule later this month. (RTRS)  

OpenAI has notified more than 100 organisations about unauthorised activity involving its AI agents, Reuters reports. The company is reviewing roughly 50 petabytes of data following the Hugging Face incident, which remains the most severe case it has identified. (RTRS)   

OpenAI fired three safety researchers over alleged misconduct including sharing confidential information with an outside AI-safety organisation, according to WSJ sources. OpenAI confirmed the dismissals for breaches of its information-handling policies. (WSJ)  

Nike forecast a high-single-digit FY2027 sales decline versus a 2.4% drop expected and announced restructuring targeting $2.5bn of savings over five years. Shares fell 8.5% after hours following quarterly revenue of $11.2bn, down 4% and below estimates. (BBG)  

ON Semiconductor revised its Synaptics acquisition to $123/share in cash, valuing the deal at about $5.7bn versus the original $7bn stock agreement. ON expects immediate adjusted-EPS accretion; Synaptics rose 16% and ON gained 6.9% after hours. (WSJ)  

FHFA plans to require credit data from only two bureaus rather than three for mortgages sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, according to a Bloomberg source. An announcement could come on 12 October; Equifax and TransUnion fell 5.9% and 4.7% respectively after hours. (BBG)  

RTX won a US Navy contract worth up to $24.4bn to increase SM-6 missile production. The agreement runs for five years with a two-year option, as the Pentagon seeks to replenish weapons stocks depleted by the Iran war. (BBG)  

UK PM Andy Burnham’s focus on buying British has added urgency to UK government reviews of Palantir contracts with the NHS and Ministry of Defence. Ministers are weighing political backlash against Palantir over its US and Israeli ties and exploring British alternatives such as Quantexa, or a temporary extension. (FT)

Twilio will replace Warner Bros. Discovery in the S&P 500 before the October 6 open, S&P Dow Jones Indices announced. WBD’s removal follows its pending acquisition by Paramount Skydance. (S&P DJI) 

Moderna will replace Warner Bros. Discovery in the Nasdaq-100 effective October 9, Nasdaq announced. (RTRS)   

Comcast’s NBCUniversal is cutting jobs in its global streaming-technology organisation, primarily at Sky alongside some US positions. The final number depends on employee consultations, according to a Reuters source. (RTRS)  

Toshiba plans to double HDD production capacity for AI data centres by FY2027, investing around ¥60bn in its Philippines operations, Nikkei reports. It would be the company’s first major HDD investment in roughly five years. (Nikkei)  

Chinese EV sales disappointed during September’s traditional peak season: BYD’s growth slowed to 17%, while XPeng and Li Auto deliveries fell roughly 1% and 6.3%. Nomura said domestic demand and orders were weaker than expected, with no seasonal uplift. (WSJ)  

Volvo Cars said on Friday it will not fulfil its previous full-year outlook statements on volume and cash flow due to an increasingly challenging market situation and deteriorating near term outlook. (RTRS)

Nvidia-backed Firmus priced its Australian IPO at A$11 a share, implying a A$43.7bn valuation versus earlier expectations of up to A$50bn, according to terms seen by Bloomberg. Bookbuilding runs 6–9 October, with an ASX debut targeted for 23 October. (BBG)

text:
the most influential family. “The LORD your God shall choose.” Centralized worship would train Israel that access to God operates according to divine appointment. The people were not free to establish competing sanctuaries wherever the landscape felt inspirational. God would identify His chosen place and put His name there.

That principle puts divine authority ahead of human preference. Men naturally prefer religion customized to taste. One tribe might like a mountain. Another might prefer a grove. Another might want the sanctuary closer to home. Somebody would surely propose multiple locations for convenience. But worship was not being organized around customer satisfaction. God chose. Israel sought. Israel came. That order matters. Biblical worship begins with revelation, not market research. When churches begin asking what men want before asking what God said, they have already changed who occupies the throne.

Eventually Jerusalem would become uniquely identified with God’s chosen sanctuary, though Deuteronomy 12 speaks prospectively before the final location is historically established. The central point remains: God determines the place of worship under Israel’s covenant. The Church today does not inherit Jerusalem’s temple system. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the hour was coming when worship would not be centered in that mountain or Jerusalem in the old covenant manner, and then said, “the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (John 4:21–23). Different dispensation, same principle of divine definition: worship must be according to truth.

6. Bring the Offerings Where God Commands

Verse 6 specifies what Israel is to bring: “your burnt offerings, and your sacrifices, and your tithes, and heave offering of your hand, and your vows, and your freewill offerings, and the firstlings of your herds and of your flocks.” The list is extensive because Israel’s worship under the law involved real sacrifices, gifts, vows, and sacred obligations. But these offerings were not merely valuable because Israel gave them. Their acceptability depended upon being offered according to God’s order. A sincere sacrifice in the wrong system was still wrong. An expensive offering does not bribe holiness.

This is another rebuke to religious self-confidence. Men frequently imagine that cost proves legitimacy. If someone gave much, sacrificed greatly, traveled far, or endured hardship, surely God must be impressed. Yet Scripture never teaches that sacrifice itself sanctifies error. The prophets repeatedly confronted people who multiplied offerings while living in rebellion. Isaiah records God saying, “To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me?” (Isaiah 1:11). Ritual abundance cannot compensate for disobedience. A thousand wrong offerings do not eventually add up to one right act of worship. Quantity cannot repair contradiction.

For the Christian, Christ has fulfilled the sacrificial shadows in a way animal offerings never could. Hebrews declares that “by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). The believer therefore does not bring burnt offerings to a Mosaic sanctuary. Yet worship still requires truth. Romans 12:1 calls believers to present their bodies “a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” Notice again the word “acceptable.” Christian worship is not defined by whatever the worshipper happens to enjoy. God remains the One before whom worship must be acceptable.

text:
51 of 125: Deuteronomy 12:1–7 — The Place Which the Lord Shall Choose

Key Passage: Deuteronomy 12:1–7

Moses now turns from the blessing and curse of chapter 11 to the practical shape of worship inside the land Israel is about to possess. The opening words carry weight: “These are the statutes and judgments, which ye shall observe to do in the land” (Deuteronomy 12:1). Israel is not entering Canaan as spiritual tourists free to sample whatever religious customs look attractive. The land is full of altars, high places, groves, pillars, images, sacred names, and established worship traditions belonging to nations God is judging. The Israelites will be surrounded by religion, but religion itself is not automatically acceptable. God does not tell them to study the pagan systems, borrow whatever seems useful, repaint the idols, put a Hebrew label on the altar, and call the result outreach. He commands destruction. That makes Deuteronomy 12 an assault upon the notion that sincerity sanctifies worship. It does not. God decides how God is worshipped.

The doctrinal setting must remain clear. This is Israel under the Mosaic covenant entering the literal land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The chapter concerns Israel’s national worship, sacrifices, tithes, offerings, sacred meals, and the central place where the LORD would put His name. The Church is not Israel, the local church building is not the Jerusalem temple, and Christians today are not commanded to travel to a geographical sanctuary in Canaan to offer animal sacrifices. The believer worships God through Jesus Christ and is part of a heavenly people saved by grace through faith. Yet none of those dispensational distinctions weaken the principle blazing through the text: man does not possess authority to reinvent the worship of God. Right division protects the passage from misuse; it does not muzzle the rebuke.

The chapter begins, therefore, by putting human religious creativity under judgment. Canaan’s people had their places, practices, symbols, sacred objects, and spiritual traditions. Some were ancient. Some were culturally beloved. Some undoubtedly appeared beautiful. None of that mattered once God called them abominations. Age does not purify error. Popularity does not baptize false worship. Sincerity does not turn idolatry into obedience. A religious practice can have architecture, music, emotion, history, symbolism, devoted participants, and still be completely wrong. Men like to imagine that anything aimed upward eventually reaches God. Scripture presents a different picture: there is a God in heaven who has already spoken downward. The question is not whether worship feels spiritual. The question is whether the God being worshipped authorized it.

1. Destroy the Pagan Places Before They Become Israel’s Places

Moses says, “Ye shall utterly destroy all the places, wherein the nations which ye shall possess served their gods” (Deuteronomy 12:2). The command is not mild. God does not say to regulate those sites, preserve them as museums, or keep a few for comparative religion. “Utterly destroy” leaves little room for sentimental preservation. The pagan worship system was embedded in the geography of Canaan, with shrines “upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree.” Israel was entering a land where false religion had claimed the scenery itself. God commanded them to remove its visible infrastructure so that yesterday’s idolatry would not become tomorrow’s temptation.

Stop Dolling Around And Be Serious! 

The seven angels. 
Revelation 15:1 And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvellous, seven angels having the seven last plagues; for in them is filled up the wrath of God.
(This is the cup that Jesus was talking about in Matthew 26(39); Mark 14(36); Luke 22(42); John 18(11). Jeremiah also mentioned it. Jer. 25(15). )

Worship offered. 
Revelation 15:2 And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.
(What’s fire? James 3(6); John 1(1); Hebrews 12(29); Exodus 3(2). What is the mark of the beast 666? Rev, 13(17); Gen. 4(15, 23, 24); Daniel 7(7, 8). )
Revelation 15:3 And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, 
(Deuteronomy 32. )
and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and marvellous are Thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are Thy ways, Thou King of saints. 
(saints = set aside ones. See Romans 11. )
Revelation 15:4 Who shall not fear Thee, O Lord, and glorify Thy name? for Thou only art holy: for all nations shall come and worship before Thee; for Thy judgments are made manifest.” 
(Judgements on earth are clearly seen in the eyes of those who have eyes to see. Thy name = The Word of God. Rev. 19(-13). )

The seven angels. 
Revelation 15:5 And after that I looked, and, behold, the Temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven was opened:
(Not on earth. The Temple : includes the Holy of the Holies. See note on Matthew 23(16) in the companion Bible. )
Revelation 15:6 And the seven angels came out of the Temple, having the seven plagues, clothed in pure and white linen, and having their breasts girded with golden girdles.
(girdles = Ephesians 6(14-). Linen : Rev. 19(8). )
Revelation 15:7 And one of the four beasts gave unto the seven angels seven golden vials full of the wrath of God, who liveth for ever and ever.
(seven golden vials full of the wrath of God = the wrath of the Creator. )

Worship no longer possible. 
Revelation 15:8 And the Temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God, and from His power; and no man was able to enter into the Temple, till the seven plagues of the seven angels were fulfilled.
(7 vials of Rev. 16, 17. )

text:
After descending the mountain from Temple 21, Tairyūji,
we arrive at Temple 22, Byōdōji.

This peaceful temple sits at the foot of the mountains in Anan City, Tokushima.
Passing through its impressive temple gate,
you will find Yakushi Nyorai enshrined in the main hall.

One of the highlights is “Kōbō’s Sacred Spring,”
said to have been dug by Kobo Daishi himself.

The water still flows today and is cherished by many visitors.
The Daishi Hall is also home to a rare statue of one of Kobo Daishi’s disciples.

After completing the demanding mountain sections around Temples 20 and 21,
Byōdōji offers a sense of accomplishment and a welcome moment to reset.

Before continuing to the next temple,
why not take some time here to refresh both body and mind?

text:
After trade war, capital war?

Whether the AI bubble bursts or the borrowing binge continues, India will need to strengthen its defences

by T N Ninan

In the retreat from globalisation, the world has already seen multiplying restrictions on the cross-border movement of people. Since Donald Trump’s return to the US presidency and the advent of tariffs as a coercive instrument of policy, the global trade in goods and services has also taken a hit. What may come next are restrictions by rich countries on the international movement of capital (capital controls have long been the norm in developing countries).

The primary provocation for such a radical move (unthinkable till just the other day) lies in the United States (US), where the irresistible force of growing corporate borrowings is up against the immovable object of the US budget deficit. The big corporations leading the tech and artificial intelligence (AI) race were until recently financing their capital budgets out of their earnings. No longer, as investment plans have ballooned. Now they are borrowing in the market, and borrowing big as corporate bond issuances in the US have grown 80 per cent in two years. At the same time, the federal deficit has grown to 7 per cent of gross domestic product, and shows no sign of coming under control.

US savings aren’t anywhere near enough to feed these hungry beasts, which is why the US has been for decades the world’s biggest borrower. But its growing need for capital from other countries is up against the fact that almost all large countries are turning away from US securities. China has halved its US holdings in the last few years, while Japan (now the largest holder of US securities) has started moving away too. The total foreign holdings of marketable US Treasuries are down to 30 per cent of the total, from 50 per cent in 2015. Even as central banks reduce their dollar holdings, they have increased the share of gold in their reserves. Last year, gold replaced US government bonds as the largest reserve asset; the price of gold has increased by 25 per cent in a year (and Indians are still big-time buyers!).

With increasing dollar-debt issuances in the face of fading appetite for such debt, the inevitable has happened — interest rates have gone up. US Treasury rates are now the highest in two decades, and climbing. Yet international bidders for fresh US debt now account for a smaller part of the market than before. Five-year Treasury interest rates have gone up by 0.64 per cent in just one month. The US Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, has spent the past few weeks trying a variety of gambits to talk the market down, to no effect.

If, despite higher rates, the US doesn’t get the capital that it wants from other countries, it could simply print dollars, cause inflation as more money chases the same goods, and thereby reduce the debt burden in real (ie inflation-adjusted) terms.  India has done this for decades. In fact, as Western country debts have grown, inflation in the last five years in the US has been more than twice as high as in the previous decade, in Europe three times as high, and in Japan five times as high. Inflation wars to control debt, you might say.

There is also the possibility (still remote but real) that the US might turn coercive on capital, as it has on trade. Already, Mr Trump has made investment commitments a part of some of his bilateral trade deals. Today, he is coercing inflow. Tomorrow he may squeeze outflow.

In anticipation, some countries have started taking defensive measures. The Netherlands moved 78 tonnes of gold from New York to London in the last few months. The explanation was possible “geopolitical unrest”. Shortly before that, France moved all its gold out of the US. There are calls in Germany to do the same. Unthinkable as it may have been not long ago, trust in the continued openness of the US capital market has begun to erode at the margins.
Meanwhile, expert voices in Europe have called for disincentivising the movement of European capital to the US, since Europe needs to invest in itself. Any such move by Europe will almost certainly be met by a counter-move from Washington. A headline in the Financial Times said in early September that “The capital wars are coming”.

All this should be of serious concern to India. Portfolio capital has been moving out of the country for the last couple of years, and the rupee has taken a tumble, falling 13 per cent in value despite active Reserve Bank intervention, even as rising energy prices affect the trade balance. It is no coincidence that the main stock market indices are back to where they were two-and-a-half years ago. The last time the market disappointed investors over an extended period was in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.

The biggest Reserve Bank initiative in the face of these trends was to offer a huge free lunch to non-resident Indians: Deposits at attractive interest rates along with currency protection. It may have overplayed its hand, because the scheme brought in twice as much money as was expected, over $130 billion. Non-resident Indians (NRIs) can obviously recognise a free lunch when they are offered one. The cost of the scheme to the RBI  will depend on how currency rates move, and could be between $10 billion and $20 billion over the course of the scheme.

Naturally, there have been critics who have made two arguments. First, the foreign-exchange reserves position is comfortable, which was not the case when attractive deposit terms were offered to NRIs in the past, through the Millennium Bonds and Resurgent India Bonds. Second, the terms of the offer were needlessly generous. The second argument holds more water than the first, because the uncertainty and tensions in international capital markets warranted a precautionary move of some kind.

Consider that, in the six months between the end of February (when the US attacked Iran) and the end of August, the RBI’s foreign exchange reserves went up by a little over $50 billion, though about $130 billion came in as  foreign currency non-resident (bank), or FCNR(B), deposits during this period. Neither the current account deficit nor net capital flows can fully explain the missing $80 billion. It is obvious that the RBI has spent a lot of dollars  shoring up the rupee as capital has gone out of the country. So getting some extra dollars as a cushion can do no harm.

Two scenarios are now possible. 

If the AI investment bubble bursts, there will be a global tsunami, since the US stock market accounts for more than two-thirds of global market capitalisation. 

If not, and the borrowing binge by governments and companies continues, there will be unprecedented competition for capital, leading to possibly higher inflation and/or restrictions on cross-country capital flows. 

It makes sense, therefore, to shore up reserves, increase economic security by reducing the budget deficit and government debt, and make the country more attractive to investors. 

The additional reserves can be used to fight currency volatility, and to fund any capital outflows. They can also be used to boost confidence in the economy’s external solvency at a time when no one knows how exactly the cards will fall.

The writer is former editor and former chairman of Business Standard

text:
Honestly, this is not the kind of story Nigerians should read and celebrate as another example of somebody “hustling” abroad.

There is something deeply shameful about it, but the shame should not primarily be placed on the person begging.

The bigger shame belongs to a country that has repeatedly failed to create an environment where ordinary people can work honestly, earn enough to live with dignity, build a modest home, raise children and support ageing parents.

Think about the contradiction for a moment.

According to this post, begging on the streets of Italy became economically useful enough for someone to support a family back home and build a house.

Whether every detail of the viral story is accurate or not, the fact that Nigerians can recognise the economic desperation behind it should trouble us.

We come from a country blessed with enormous human talent, natural resources and entrepreneurial energy.

Nigerians work hard.

Anyone who has lived here knows that.

People wake up before sunrise, sit in Lagos traffic, run businesses with unreliable infrastructure, combine two or three sources of income and still struggle to stay financially afloat.

So when travelling abroad to beg can begin to look more rewarding than holding down legitimate work at home, something is seriously wrong.

And this is where governance enters the conversation.

Bad governance is not only about politicians stealing money or another corruption scandal appearing in the news.

Bad governance eventually becomes personal.

It is the graduate who cannot find sustainable work.

It is the small business owner spending scarce money providing basic infrastructure.

It is the family watching the cost of everyday necessities stretch household income beyond its limits.

It is also the Nigerian who concludes that almost anything abroad offers a better chance of survival than staying home.

That is what makes stories like this humiliating for us.

Not because Nigerians are somehow above begging, and certainly not because poverty should make anybody less human.

There is dignity in every human life.

But there is no dignity in a system that leaves citizens feeling that humiliation abroad may offer greater economic security than opportunity at home.

We should also be careful not to romanticise suffering by calling everything a "hustle."

Survival is not always success.

Sometimes survival is simply evidence of how badly circumstances have failed somebody.

The painful question is therefore not, "How could a Nigerian spend nine years begging in Italy?"

The more important question is, "What kind of Nigeria are we building when something like this can appear to be a sensible economic choice?"

Until governance begins to translate Nigeria's wealth and potential into decent jobs, functioning public services, economic stability and genuine opportunity for ordinary people, stories like this will continue to embarrass us.

The individual in this story should not carry Nigeria's shame alone.

Our greater shame is that, after all these years, too many Nigerians still have to leave home simply to find a fighting chance at life.

AJD.

Alinsky analysis - On October 1, 2026, in Lakeland, JD Vance said that if Angie Nixon calls herself a socialist, the right reply is “get the hell out of here. You don’t belong in America.” Nixon, the Democratic Senate nominee in Florida and a recent DSA member, answered by invoking her ancestors and the buildings they helped raise. Ro Khanna then framed the line as Vance telling “a Black woman who is a descendant of enslaved people” to leave America. @BloodEnglish replied that Vance never addressed a “Black woman,” that Khanna was being racist, and that the target was a “loudmouth, asshole, DSA, America-hating, communist, freak show,” treated as any similar “low life” would be.

Five of Alinsky’s tactics are in play. 
Rule 13 freezes and polarizes the target: Nixon is no longer a racial descendant but a communist freak, and Khanna becomes the liar. 
Rule 5 uses ridicule—“freak show,” “asshole,” “low life”—which is hard to answer without amplifying it. 
Rule 4 forces the other side to live by its own book: if judging people by race is racist, then racializing Vance’s attack is racist. 
Rule 3 leaves the opponent’s ground (slavery, identity) for ideology and conduct. 
Rule 11 pushes the charge of racism until it is meant to flip onto the accuser.

As a tactic the reply is coherent and on-brand for its audience. As a result it is weak. It offers no constructive alternative (Rule 12), applies no sustained pressure (Rules 8 and 10), and reached only a few hundred views. It can satisfy allies; it does not shift the larger frame Khanna set.

🟣 USDAI: a new TVL ATH on the way?

After a sharp drop earlier this year, @USDai_Official's TVL is recovering.

The protocol's total TVL now stands at over $650M, after a previous record of $690M set in November 2025.

What's interesting in this data is that the share of unstaked base:0x0a1a1a107e45b7ced86833863f482bc5f4ed82ef keeps shrinking over time. This means that mercenary capital, which was only there to farm as many points as possible ahead of the airdrops and the $CHIP token ICO, is moving away. The protocol can therefore focus more on what gives it its real added value: GPU-backed loans.

👉 This is good news for the few stakers who had taken advantage of this mercenary capital to capture yield in late 2025, since ethereum:0x0b2b2b2076d95dda7817e785989fe353fe955ef9 yields had dropped once that capital left.

The growth in sUSDai TVL, directly correlated with the increase in the total amount lent out, should logically allow USDAI to offer more attractive yields. The net yield currently stands at 7.26%, so we should probably expect it to climb over the coming weeks.

Meanwhile, several factors could support the protocol's growth:

text:
Lil Wayne refusing to put his cup down made more sense once he explained what quitting felt like. "Feels like death in your stomach when you stop," he told MTV in 2008. The drink in that cup had already killed two of the rappers who made it famous.

The cup held lean, prescription promethazine-codeine cough syrup poured into soda. Codeine converts to morphine in your liver. Promethazine deepens the sedation and slows your breathing further, which is why overdoses tend to kill people in their sleep.

DJ Screw built an entire genre around the drink, slowing Houston rap down to match its effect. He died of a codeine overdose in 2000 at age 29.

Pimp C recorded "Sippin' on Some Syrup," the song that took the drink national. He died in 2007 when the syrup combined with his sleep apnea.

Wayne watched both happen and kept sipping. In 2013 a string of seizures put him in a Los Angeles ICU, where doctors reportedly pumped his stomach three times after finding high amounts of codeine in his system.

Then the manufacturer did something no drug company had done before. In 2014 Actavis shut down all production and sales of its syrup, saying celebrity attention had glamorized the product. A pint was selling for $800 on the street before the shutdown, and afterward one rapper reportedly offered his dealer $100,000 for whatever bottles were left.

A drug company walked away from a profitable product because rap made it too famous. The drink killed the man who invented its sound and the man who wrote its anthem. Wayne kept sipping until the manufacturer quit before he did.

text:
The essence of government is to plan, invest, and care for the people.

The only way a state makes money is not through Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) and federal allocations alone. A responsible government should also diversify the state's economy and create multiple sources of sustainable revenue.

As Governor of Anambra State, Peter Obi diversified the state's economy and made investments aimed at creating additional sources of income for the state.

Apart from the state's existing IGR and federal allocations, his administration invested ₦4.4 billion in direct and indirect project expenditure and contributions to the Orient Petroleum project. The state also has a recorded investment/shareholding in Orient Petroleum valued at ₦573 million.

Peter Obi also invited the then President, Goodluck Jonathan, to commission the Orient Petroleum facilities, marking an important milestone in Anambra's emergence as an oil-producing state.

Today, Anambra State receives 13% derivation revenue from oil production and remains an investor in Orient Petroleum.

Peter Obi's $156 million was not simply sitting idle as cash. It was invested in financial instruments to generate returns for Anambra State. According to Obi, these investments were capable of generating about $10 million annually for the state.

This is what good governance should be about: not just spending government revenue, but saving, investing, diversifying the economy, and creating sustainable sources of income for future generations.

Peter Obi may not be perfect, but I believe his approach to saving, investment, and economic diversification offers important lessons for Nigeria.

I believe Peter Obi could be one of the best things that could happen to Nigeria, and I hope that, as people examine the records and evidence for themselves, they will understand why I support him.

A new Nigeria is POssible and Nigeria will be OK ✌️

Alyssa McGrath:

An executive assistant since May 2018 & Brittany Commisso's high school best friend. Also going thru a divorce, she came out with her story 10 days after Commisso, acting as the only individual to back up Commisso's character. She alleged "unwanted attention" in the form of "ogling" & suggestive comments, admitting she only found the interactions troubling "after the fact" once the broader political operation against Cuomo began.

The AG report cited an early 2019 incident where McGrath claimed she bent forward during dictation & felt Cuomo was staring down her loose blouse before asking about her necklace. Cuomo testified that asking about the necklace—an Italian horn—was standard social behavior since they both shared Italian heritage. & photos of the Executive Chamber layout demonstrated that the structural depth & angle of the Governor’s desk made it physically impossible to look down an employee's shirt from across the room. Her family member, Matt McGrath, later revealed that Alyssa routinely wore low-cut tops & had systematically deleted photos of herself in those outfits from her social media accounts immediately after filing her claims.

Complained that Cuomo asked if she spoke Italian, said something in the language, & "grinned." Her father later guessed the comment meant she was beautiful, which made her feel uncomfortable. Investigators never interviewed her father or clarified what was actually said.

Ana Liss: Claimed harassment bc Cuomo called her "sweetheart," kissed her hand, & noticed a run in her pantyhose during a presentation. Public records noted that Liss kept a large, framed photo of Cuomo prominently displayed on her desk long after she stopped working for him. She was among the accusers directly targeted & whipped up by Lindsey Boylan to add bulk to the narrative.

Kaitlin M: Claimed harassment bc Cuomo told her to "soak up knowledge like a sponge" & bc he declined to take her personal cell number when she offered it to him. She had many documented workplace performance issues, eg repeatedly getting in trouble for dropping vital Governor calls. She was also contacted & recruited by Lindsey Boylan to join the public push.

Virginia Limmiatis: Didn’t work for Cuomo but claimed that at a May 2017 public event, he pressed his fingers against her shirt & read its logo, & whispered a cover story about a spider on her shoulder as an excuse to brush against her. She claimed 4 years later that reviewing event photos brought back a "flood of negative emotions." Bc she was never a state employee, workplace harassment laws did not apply. Official event photos from the Governor’s Flickr archive entirely disproved her timeline: there was no rope line as she claimed, Cuomo’s hands were visibly nowhere near her chest, & Limmiatis was pictured smiling happily while placing her own hand on Cuomo’s shoulder, lingering afterward to take photos of him. The Oswego DA dismissed the case.

The State Trooper: Alleges Cuomo touched her belly while she held open a door as he passed by, touched her back in an elevator, & kissed her on the cheek after she consented. Cuomo's legal team submitted extensive photographic proof of his routine public "hug & kiss culture," demonstrating he used these greetings uniformly with male & female politicians alike. All 3 claims were systematically dismissed by 3 separate District Attorneys.

Anonymous State Employee: Alleged that Cuomo touched her butt during a work event. The evidence was found to be entirely inconsistent with the AG's own compiled text, & the Manhattan DA dismissed the claim.

Elizabeth Dufort: A nurse who quit her job because she disagreed with the admin’s vaccine plan. Her formal harassment complaint consisted of Cuomo jokingly telling her, "You make this gown look good," while she was administering a standard covid test to him.

Eating keto after 60 should not feel confusing, extreme, or impossible.

If you are curious about low-carb living but feel overwhelmed by strict rules, complicated recipes, or loud promises online, this gentle guide was created for you. Keto for Seniors After 60 offers a calm, practical, senior-friendly approach to keto, focused on simple meals, real ingredients, and a lifestyle that can actually fit everyday life.

This is not an aggressive diet book. It does not promise miracles, cures, or overnight transformations. Instead, it helps you understand how to reduce sugar and refined carbohydrates in a realistic way, while building satisfying plates with protein, low-carb vegetables, healthy fats, and easy everyday recipes.

Inside this book, you will discover:

A simple explanation of keto in everyday language

How eating after 60 can be different from eating at 30 or 40

How to build a safe, satisfying senior keto plate

Easy low-carb pantry swaps for bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, and sweets

Calm breakfast ideas, simple lunches, comforting dinners, and small treats

Air fryer and one-pan keto meals for easier cooking and less cleanup

Hydration, electrolytes, fiber, and digestion tips for a gentler transition

Shopping ideas for one or two people without wasting food

How to handle restaurants, holidays, and family meals without stress

A practical 30-day senior keto meal plan to help you get started

Troubleshooting guidance for cravings, stalls, boredom, and common mistakes

This book is especially helpful for seniors, beginners, and adults over 60 who want a clear and manageable way to explore keto without feeling pressured to be perfect.

You do not need a kitchen full of expensive ingredients. You do not need to cook complicated meals. You do not need to change everything overnight.

You only need a calmer plan, familiar foods, and a gentle place to begin.

Keto for Seniors After 60 is your practical companion for creating easier low-carb meals, simplifying your kitchen, and building a sustainable way of eating that feels realistic, nourishing, and respectful of your stage of life.

Educational note: This book is for informational purposes only and does not replace medical advice. Seniors and anyone with medical conditions or medications should speak with a qualified healthcare professional before starting a strict keto or low-carb diet.

On September 30, the eve of the feast of St. Thérèse of Lisieux, Tennessee failed to execute Christa Gail Pike.

After two doses of lethal injection, she remained alive. Officials took her to a hospital. The Governor then halted all remaining executions for the year. Experts are calling it unprecedented.

Why does the date matter?

Before she became a Carmelite, 14 year old Thérèse Martin heard about Henri Pranzini, a man condemned for a brutal triple murder in Paris in 1887. He refused the chaplain and was called impenitent.

Thérèse made him her "first child." She offered Masses and prayed:

"My God, I am quite sure that Thou wilt pardon this unhappy Pranzini... but this is my first sinner, and therefore I beg for just one sign of repentance to reassure me."

On August 31, 1887, at the foot of the scaffold, Pranzini turned, seized the crucifix and kissed the wounds of Christ three times.

Thérèse wrote: "I had obtained the sign I asked for."

139 years later, on the vigil of her feast, another condemned prisoner is given more time.

The Church has not declared this a miracle. But for those who love St. Thérèse, the pattern is familiar. She did not pray that Pranzini escape justice. She prayed that he not be lost. That he be given a sign.

On September 30, justice was suspended, not to deny accountability, but perhaps to extend mercy.

October 2, 1780 — Hanging of Major John André. In Tappan, New York, Continental forces hanged André as a spy. He was Benedict Arnold's contact in the plot to turn West Point over to the British. Militia stopped him on September 23 near Tarrytown (right next to now named, Sleepy Hollow) with incriminating papers hidden in his boot; Arnold escaped aboard the HMS Vulture. A board of generals led by Nathanael Greene found André guilty.

Washington refused his request to be shot as a soldier rather than hanged, and offered to spare him only in exchange for Arnold, which the British declined. André was buried near the gallows; his remains were later moved to Westminster Abbey in
1821. Contemporary accounts note that he met the death calmly and was widely regretted even among American officers.

This is the self portrait he drew awaiting his hanging.

WWE Details How Its Gorilla Position Actually Works
Bill Pritchard
Tue, July 29, 2025 at 10:35 AM PDT
WWE is giving fans an "unreal" look at what goes on behind the scenes.

WWE: Unreal premiered on Netflix on Tuesday. The new docuseries gives fans an inside look at the inner workings of WWE creative. During one episode, @WWE  detailed how its "Gorilla position" functions during a WWE television taping. The "Gorilla position" refers to the backstage area just behind the stage. It functions as a control center for the show, and got its name as a tribute to the late Gorilla Monsoon.

"The Gorilla position is very unique. In every arena, it's custom-built. However, the inside and the workings of it are the same," Bruce Prichard said during a voiceover.

"There's primarily three tables set up inside Gorilla position," said WWE SVP of Creative Writing, Ed Koskey. "[It's] one table where @TripleH  and Bruce Prichard are sitting. There's another table where Billy Kidman, who is our producer responsible for timing out the show and keeping tabs on times, [will sit]. Next to him will sit the respective match producer."

"It's a whole other world in my earpiece"
Koskey highlighted all of the WWE producers being former in-ring talent, naming Park, Bobby Roode and Michael Hayes as producers, along with Prichard as the executive head of creative.

Chris Park (aka TNA's Abyss) described his job as being a liaison between talent and the heads of creative, Triple H and Bruce Prichard. Park said he also communicates with the production truck to try and stay about 15 seconds ahead so they are in position to get the right camera shots.

"Another thing I am doing on that headset as well is I'm talking to the referees. The referees can hear me," Park explained.

Robert James "Gino" Marella (June 4, 1937 – October 6, 1999), better known by his ring name, Gorilla Monsoon, was an American professional wrestler, play-by-play commentator, and booker.

Monsoon is famous for his run as a villainous super-heavyweight main eventer, and later as the voice of the World Wrestling Federation (WWF), as commentator and backstage manager during the 1980s and 1990s. He also portrayed the on-screen role of WWF President from 1995 to 1997.

In professional wrestling, the staging area just behind the entrance curtain at an event, a position which Marella established and where he could often be found during WWF shows late in his career, is named the "Gorilla Position" in his honor.

Personal life and death
Marella was married to his wife, Maureen (née Hess)(1939–2025), for more than 40 years and had four children: Sharon (born 1960), Joey (1963–1994), and Valerie (born 1966). Víctor Quiñones (1959–2006) was listed in Gorilla's obituary as his son as well.[11] However, Marella's family denies that Quiñones was a biological child of Marella.[12]

On July 4, 1994, his son, Joey Marella, who worked as a referee for the WWF, fell asleep at the wheel and died in a car accident on the New Jersey Turnpike while returning from refereeing an event in Ocean City, Maryland. He was not wearing a seatbelt at the time of the crash.[4] Fellow WWF employee Mike Chioda later commented that Marella was "heartbroken" about his son's death.[13]

In early 1994, Marella co-hosted the short-lived morning variety/game show Bingo Break on WBFF in Baltimore, Maryland, which also featured fellow WWF on-air personality Sean Mooney as the bingo caller. The program did not acknowledge Marella's wrestling career, and as such he was billed on-camera as Bob Marella rather than as Gorilla Monsoon.[14]

Death
Marella died on October 6, 1999, of heart failure brought on by complications of diabetes, at his home in Willingboro Township, New Jersey.[15] He was 62 years old. His body was buried next to his son, Joey Marella, at Lakeview Memorial Park in Cinnaminson, New Jersey.

He was elevated to the College of Cardinals in 1959 by Pope John XXIII and returned to Rome in 1960 to join the curia. Joseph Anthony Marella (February 28, 1963 – July 4, 1994) was an American professional wrestling referee for the World Wrestling Federation and son of former wrestler and then WWF announcer Gorilla Monsoon (Robert Marella) from Willingboro Township, New Jersey.[1]

Career
Joey Marella joined the World Wrestling Federation in 1983,[2] and moved through the ranks until he was often assigned to referee feature promotion matches.[3] In 1987, he served as the referee for the much-hyped match between Hulk Hogan and André the Giant at WrestleMania III as well as their rematch in 1988 at WrestleMania IV.[4] 10 minutes prior to their WrestleMania III match, André had asked Vince McMahon to choose Marella to be the referee for that match.[5]

Marella was also the official for the 1992 SummerSlam main event of Bret Hart vs. Davey Boy Smith at London's famous Wembley Stadium.[6] Marella was briefly suspended for a substance abuse problem in 1993 and then later re-hired.[7]

He was also part of the controversy at the 1994 Royal Rumble match in which he and former WWF referee Earl Hebner couldn't decide between Lex Luger and Bret Hart as to who had won the match.[8][9][10]

During Marella's career as a WWF referee, while becoming one of the Federation's most respected in-ring officials, he also became the butt of jokes for heel based commentators especially when they were teamed with Marella's father Gorilla Monsoon with Monsoon regularly using one of his catch phrases "Will you stop" (mostly said to either Jesse "The Body" Ventura or Bobby "The Brain" Heenan) when they would criticize his performance. This was actually an inside joke, as the fact that Monsoon and Marella were actually father and son was not well known by fans until after Marella had died. Earl Hebner discussed in an interview how Marella was a good person. Hebner revealed that he was scheduled to referee the last match on a card, but Marella offered to referee the last match so Hebner could get out early and fly home from the nearby Newark Airport.[11]

Other media
Marella also appeared in the 1989 WWF produced movie No Holds Barred as a referee during a wrestling match.[12]

Death and legacy
He died in a car accident on July 4, 1994, at the age of 31, after he fell asleep at the wheel and crashed into a guardrail and a tree while driving home on the New Jersey Turnpike after a night of refereeing WWF matches in Ocean City, Maryland.[13][14][15] Bruno Lauer, better known by his ring name Harvey Wippleman, was with him at the time and was critically injured. Lauer was wearing a seatbelt, while Marella was not. Following his death, the WWF instituted rules that WWF personnel had to check into hotels when working late. Furthermore, they would no longer travel alone and everyone traveling together had to agree to travel.[16] Marella is buried next to his father Gorilla Monsoon (1937–1999) at Lakeview Memorial Park in Cinnaminson, New Jersey. Images of a baseball player and a golfer were placed on his headstone due to his love of the two sports.[2] As a tribute, WWE ring announcer Tony Chimel named his son after Marella. Marella's sister Valerie also named a son after her brother.[1]

What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

Victors narrative I'm afraid, just like 9-11, Gaza, WW2 is in a class of its own though; 
The war was not launched to murder Poles. Versailles had cut the Corridor through Germany and detached Danzig, a city about 96 percent German. On 24 October 1938 Ribbentrop offered Lipski four points: Danzig returned to the Reich with Polish free-port rights retained; no demand for the Corridor itself, only an extraterritorial road and railway to East Prussia; a permanent border guarantee; and extension of the 1934 pact to twenty-five years. Henderson called Hitler the most moderate German on Danzig and the Corridor. Beck was given the same guarantee at Berchtesgaden on 5 January 1939. Poland refused. Chamberlain’s blank-cheque guarantee of 31 March, urged on by Roosevelt and Bullitt, made refusal costless. Polish papers had already written of a new Grunwald “in the suburbs of Berlin” and of a war with “no prisoners” and “no room for human feelings.” Rydz-Śmigły is quoted as saying Poland wanted war with Germany and that Germany would not be able to avoid it. Britain and France then declared war on Germany and said nothing when the Red Army entered eastern Poland on 17 September.
The charge that Germans uniquely murdered Christian women and children inverts the documented sequence. Bradberry records the pre-war terror against the German minority in the Corridor, including Bromberg (“Bloody Sunday”): an estimated 5,500 ethnic Germans killed in that massacre alone, with children nailed to barns, women raped and axed, and 328 people burned in the Protestant church; he puts the wider toll of German nationals killed by Polish mobs near 58,000. Irving independently records that the local Polish commander at Bydgoszcz ordered the massacre of several thousand German residents, and that German medical units and captured paratroopers were shot. German reprisals followed a guerrilla war that Colonel Eduard Wagner, on 4 September 1939, called already general: emergency courts, death sentences, “the harder we strike, the quicker there will be peace.” That is occupation warfare against an armed population, not a program aimed at Christian civilians as such. The same victors’ narrative that calls Germans subhuman is silent on Allied area bombing of German cities and on the Soviet deportations and Katyn shootings. Irving notes that the diaries and letters on the Polish officers opened in 1943 were last dated April 1940, when the region was under Soviet control.
On occupation policy itself, Irving is explicit and limited. Hitler’s August aim was destruction of the Polish armed forces, not a line on the map. By early September he spoke of a rump Polish state for the ethnic Poles, with the intelligentsia “extracted and accommodated elsewhere” so that no new chauvinist leadership could form. He wanted guerrillas shot summarily, and he told the army not to interfere with SS task forces charged with political security in the rear. Canaris recorded Keitel’s phrase “demographic extermination” for the parallel civil authorities; Heydrich spoke of mopping up Jewry, intelligentsia, clergy, and nobility. Wagner’s diary line that Hitler and Göring meant to “destroy and exterminate the Polish nation” is second-hand and was not committed to an order. Himmler, in surviving notes of March 1940, distinguished German policy from what he called the Bolshevik method — downright extermination of minority races — and called that method “impossible.” Executions of resistance leaders, clergy, and nobility are in the record. A demonstrated order to kill three million Polish Christians is not.
The child claim is the same pattern. Postwar Polish commissions, under the same authorities who blamed Katyn on Germany until 1990, produced round figures of “hundreds of thousands” kidnapped or sent to camps. What the contemporary record supports is selective transfer of children judged of Germanic stock — orphans of the 1939 fighting and children of arrested resistance families — into German homes and Lebensborn institutions, plus ordinary confinement of political suspects. That is not a Hitler order to murder Christian children, and it is not audited by uncontaminated primary sources at the scale claimed. Camps held resistance prisoners and, later, labor categories. They were not a machine constructed to liquidate Polish Christendom.
Bradberry’s conclusion follows from the documents: a settlement limited to Danzig and a road across the Corridor would have taken nothing from Poland. The refusal, stiffened in London and Washington, produced the campaign, the Soviet share of the killing and deportations, the reprisals, and then half a century of occupation. The round figure of three million Christian dead is the ledger of that war as written by the victors, not a body count from a German extermination order

Israelis are a nation of heroes. That might sound like a slogan, but every so often something happens that reminds us how true this is.

Of all the extraordinary stories to emerge from Wednesday’s flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the one that stands out is the courage of the passengers who realized something had gone terribly wrong, forced their way into the cockpit, and helped subdue the co-pilot, who had allegedly stabbed the captain and appeared to be trying to bring down the plane.

The aircraft plunged thousands of feet; there was chaos onboard, and the passengers had no way of knowing exactly what was happening or whether they had minutes, seconds, or no time at all.

And they acted. They didn’t wait for someone to rescue them or see if everything would resolve itself on its own. They took the initiative and saved lives: not only of the passengers on board, but whatever else the plane could have taken down with it.

When we remember aircraft that have been hijacked or crashed over the years, it is difficult not to appreciate what happened aboard this flight and how there is something deeply Israeli about it.

It is part of this country’s culture: not to stand by and watch events unfold, but to run headfirst into the fire, battle, or the storm and do whatever can be done to save lives.

We have now heard some testimony from passengers aboard the flight. It is frightening and disturbing, particularly as investigators are still trying to understand what exactly happened and what the co-pilot’s motive was. But there is also something heartwarming in hearing how people responded in those terrifying moments.

They literally took charge, and, when we think about it, it is a characteristic we know all too well. Next week, Israel will mark three years since October 7. That terrible day will be seared into our collective memory as one of the greatest failures and tragedies in Israeli history. But, like with the airplane, it too was filled with stories of some of the greatest courage this country has ever seen.

There are many different kinds of heroism, and there is no need to rank them.

But it is impossible to forget the people who woke up that morning, heard that something incomprehensible was happening in the south, understood that people were in desperate need of help, and got into their cars. They took whatever weapons they had, if they had any, and drove straight into the battle.

They did not know what they would find. They did not know how many terrorists had crossed the border, where the army was, or whether they themselves would make it home. They just went.

That, to a large extent, is the story of Israel: a small country whose people are repeatedly confronted with danger and who, when the moment comes, stand up, fight and lead the charge.

It is worth thinking about that now, just weeks before Israelis go to the polls on October 27. This election will help determine the direction Israel takes after three extraordinarily difficult years. And whichever government ultimately emerges, it will inherit a country confronting a series of strategic challenges, almost none of which have truly been resolved.

Hamas still controls part of Gaza and retains weapons and military infrastructure. Hezbollah remains a threat to Israel’s north. And Iran remains locked in confrontation over its nuclear program and its wider regional capabilities.

It is true that three years after October 7, Israel has achieved amazing accomplishments, but victory, as we know too well by now, is not measured only by what an army destroys – it is also measured by what a country builds in its place.

And that is where a striking discrepancy has emerged.

Israel’s leaders have been given an extraordinary gift: a population willing to fight, to endure difficult years, and send its children to war knowing the risks and knowing, painfully, that some will not return.

Without people like that, Israel would not survive. But courage cannot only be demanded of soldiers and civilians; it must be demanded of politicians as well.
Political courage is different. It is not about charging a cockpit or running toward gunfire. It is about making difficult decisions, accepting risk, challenging traditional assumptions and, most importantly, telling the public where you actually want to take the country.

That is the question Israelis should be asking as they prepare to vote: What is the vision?

Is the future being offered to us simply one of hunkering down, a kind of super-Sparta, stronger and better armed than everyone around us but condemned to fight one war after another?

Or is there another possibility, one that recognizes the threats Israel faces, takes them seriously, and preserves overwhelming military strength, but also searches for a path toward greater security, stability, and eventually something else?

Israel’s political leaders do not need to storm a cockpit. But they do need to show some of the same courage. Instead of spending the next few weeks telling Israelis what they will never do, whom they will never sit with, and why everyone else is dangerous, they should tell us where they want to take this country.

The Israeli people have already shown that they are prepared to be brave. Now they deserve leaders brave enough to offer them a future.

Rustam Akhtyamov, Rob Vingerhoeds and Alessandro Golkar
Published Online:26 Apr 2019

This paper aims at identifying retrofitting possibilities to incorporate existing spacecraft into a network of federated satellite systems. The paper considers existing frequency regulations for the analysis in the technical domain, but does not take into consideration how complex or time-consuming any legislative changes might be. The work concludes that from a link budget point of view and existing technology, such a configuration can provide a slant range from several hundred to thousands of kilometers. The work defines models for trade-off analysis identifying correlations between satellite negotiator parameters and the number of covered satellites. Defense Primer: Directed-Energy Weapons 
Both the 2022 National Defense Strategy and the House Armed Services Committee’s bipartisan Future of Defense Task Force Report have identified directed energy as a technology that could have a significant impact on U.S. national security in the years to come. As the Department of Defense (DOD) continues to invest in directed-energy (DE) weapons, Congress may consider implications for defense authorizations, appropriations, and oversight. Overview DOD defines DE weapons as those using concentrated electromagnetic energy, rather than kinetic energy, to “incapacitate, damage, disable, or destroy enemy equipment, facilities, and/or personnel.” DE weapons include high-energy lasers (HEL) and high-powered microwave (HPM) weapons; other DE weapons, such as particle beam weapons, are outside the scope of this In Focus. HELs might be used by ground forces in short-range air defense (SHORAD), counter-unmanned aircraft systems (C-UAS), or counter-rocket, artillery, and mortar (C-RAM) missions. The weapons might be used to “dazzle” (i.e., temporarily disable) or damage satellites and sensors. This could in turn interfere with intelligence-gathering operations; military cmmunications; and positioning, navigation, and timing systems used for weapons targeting. In addition, HELs could theoretically provide options for boost-phase missile intercept, given their speed-of-light travel time; however, experts disagree on the affordability, technological feasibility, and utility of this application. In general, HELs might offer lower costs per shot and— assuming access to a sufficient power supply—deeper magazines compared with traditional munitions. (Although a number of different types of HELs exist, many of the United States’ current programs are solid state lasers, which are fueled by electrical power. As a result, the cost per shot is equivalent to the cost of the electrical power required to fire the shot.) This could in turn produce a favorable cost exchange ratio for the defender, whose marginal costs would be significantly lower than those of the aggressor.

A growing number of governors and lawmakers have taken steps to provide fuel tax relief for at least some motorists. 

Here’s a look at some of those states:

•ALABAMA: Gov. Kay Ivey issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 120 days.
•ARKANSAS: Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
•CALIFORNIA: Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an order in September allowing a sooner switch to cheaper, winter-blends of fuel.
•GEORGIA: Gov. Brian Kemp resumed a 30-day fuel tax suspension in September, marking the second installment of the tax holiday that was first offered in the spring.
•ILLINOIS: The state budget delayed a 1.3 cent gas tax increase from July 1 to Jan. 1.
•INDIANA: Gov. Mike Braun has issued multiple extensions of a fuel tax holiday, which currently runs through Nov. 4. He also issued an executive order relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel.
•KENTUCKY: Gov. Andy Beshear in May temporarily reduced the gas tax by 10 cents. That has expired, but a freeze continues on a 0.6 cent increase that had been scheduled for July 1.
•LOUISIANA: Gov. Jeff Landry issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
•MISSOURI: Gov. Mike Kehoe issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
•NEBRASKA: Gov. Jim Pillen issued an executive order in September allowing people to seek refunds of state diesel taxes for transporting crops and livestock and relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 90 days.
•NORTH CAROLINA: Gov. Josh Stein in September ordered relaxed enforcement of restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel through the end of the year.
•NORTH DAKOTA: Gov. Kelly Armstrong issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for two months.
•OHIO: Legislation signed in October by Gov. Mike DeWine suspends state fuel taxes for 90 days.
•OKLAHOMA: Gov. Kevin Stitt in September ordered relaxed enforcement of restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 120 days.
•TEXAS: Gov. Greg Abbott issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
